chapter.title: Beyond the standard: dialects and experimental Lojban

section.title: What this chapter is, and is not
section.para: experimental cmavodefined dialectsof Lojban The main reference chapters of this book teach the account of Lojban that this edition selected. Wherever they teach a rule, they also say where it comes from: a vote of the LLG or of the BPFK, a BPFK checkpoint, or established usage. Where the sources still disagree, they say that the question is open. This chapter describes something else. It describes words and grammatical variants that no official body ever adopted, but which a reader of real Lojban text will meet sooner or later.

We call a single unadopted word an experimental cmavo, and a coherent set of unadopted grammar changes a dialect. Nothing in this chapter is official, and you do not need any of it to speak or read standard Lojban. But a reference that ignored these things would not describe the language as people actually use it.

experimental cmavoword-forms reserved for Standard Lojban itself provides the space where these words live. explains that the language reserves the cmavo shapes beyond the simple assigned forms (such as the longer vowel strings in zo'oi or su'oi) for experimental use. They are grammatical word forms with no officially assigned meaning. Coining one breaks no rule, and the new word has whatever standing its users give it. The community dictionaries record such words, clearly marked as unofficial, and let their users vote on the definitions. In this chapter, every meaning given for an experimental word is the meaning of the definition that had the most votes when this edition was prepared. A vote total is a count of people who liked a definition, and nothing more; it does not make the word official, and it does not show that anybody uses it.

dotsideas dialect that the BPFK approved The boundary between experimental and adopted has moved in the past, too. This book writes every cmevla with a dot at the start and at the end. That rule began as a deliberately partisan dialect, and its name, the dot side, was a joke. It is now approved by the BPFK (see for the details).

The established corpus itself grew out of once-experimental proposals, adopted at various levels. The published records through the Logical Language Group's meeting of December 2025, however, show no official decision that changed a rule of the language after 2020, when the Group ratified the article rules (see ). The language that people speak and write has kept moving all the same, and this chapter describes some of that motion. It does not predict what any official body will do about it, and this edition does not speak for the LLG.

parsersdialect support in The sections of this chapter document two different kinds of evidence, and it pays to keep them apart. The first is usage evidence: the feature appears in genuine text or in established community writing, and not only in a dictionary entry. The second is machine support: at least one maintained parser accepts it. They answer different questions. A parser that accepts a feature shows that someone implemented it, not that anyone uses it, so machine support alone is no proof of actual use. Not every section documents both.

The standard grammar of accepts none of the words in this chapter, and the parsers that people actually run differ from one another in which of them they accept. Some accept the popular experimental cmavo by default and keep explicit switches for the dialects that change the grammar; others keep a separate experimental grammar for everything. The set of parsers in use changes from year to year, and so do their word lists, so this book does not record which tool accepts which word. We did make sure that at least one current parser accepts every example sentence printed in this chapter; a few words below have no example sentence at all, because no parser we tried would accept one. If you rely on a tool, check what it does with a word before you lean on it.

experimental cmavostatus of All of these features are unofficial. None is ratified by the LLG or approved by the BPFK, and none comes from a BPFK checkpoint. Where this chapter says that a word is common or rare, the evidence is the text of the community's chat logs, mailing lists and wiki as this edition's editors read it, together with a community count of 2015 that tallied raw occurrences of experimental words in six corpora. Raw counts include mentions of a word as well as uses of it, so they show roughly how much a word circulates and nothing about whether it has been adopted.

section.title: Quoting the outside world: zo'oi and friends
section.para: The following experimental cmavo are discussed in this section. (In the cmavo lists of this chapter, a star on a selma'o name marks an unofficial assignment. This is either an experimental selma'o, like ZOhOI*, or an experimental addition to a standard selma'o, like PA* later on.)

cmavo-entry.description: quote next word as a rafsi
selma'o named by a quoted cmavo

section.para: zo'oiStandard Lojban quotes non-Lojban material with zoi ..., which requires a delimiting word, said twice (see ). For a single foreign word that ceremony is a heavy one, and a family of experimental cmavo exists to shorten it. The word zo'oi quotes exactly one following word, just as zo does for a single Lojban word. In speech, pauses delimit the quoted word; in writing, whitespace (spaces, tabs, or line breaks) does the job:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Small is an English word.

section.para: la'oiIts sibling la'oi does the same for names, and stands to la'o as zo'oi stands to zoi. The community count of 2015 put la'oi and zo'oi at the top of its list of experimental cmavo. That is no surprise, since foreign names of one word (of people, software, and websites) are everywhere:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: I like Bach.

section.para: me'oi ra'oi Two rarer members complete the family. The word me'oi makes an ad-hoc predicate out of a foreign word. The community calls the result a stage-0 fu'ivla: a borrowing that skips even the minimal Lojbanization of :

interlinear-gloss.natlang: The horse is galloping.

section.para: And ra'oi quotes a single word as a rafsi. This is useful because many rafsi are not words at all, so zo cannot quote them:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: ra'oi bra cu rafsi zo barda
interlinear-gloss.natlang: The rafsi bra belongs to barda.

section.para: la'auNames made of Lojban words are a different problem. The article la takes a cmevla or a selbri, but a title like The Horse and the Cat is neither; it is a whole sumti, and in standard Lojban one must either rebuild it as a cmevla or quote it with la'o as if it were foreign. The word la'au opens a quotation of grammatical Lojban text, closed by the ordinary li'u, and makes a name of it. The quoted text must be grammatical on its own, as with lu (see ):

interlinear-gloss.jbo: la'au lo xirma .e lo mlatu li'u cu cmene le lisri
interlinear-gloss.gloss: [name-quote] the horse and the cat [unquote] - is-the-name-of the story.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: The Horse and the Cat is the name of the story.

section.para: ma'oiFinally, ma'oi quotes a single cmavo, like zo, and uses it to name that word's selma'o: ma'oi ba is selma'o PU, and so is ma'oi pu. This book has needed selma'o names on nearly every page, and it has borrowed capital letters to write them; ma'oi is the community's way of saying them aloud in Lojban.
Genuine text attests all six: la'oi and zo'oi heavily, la'au often, me'oi, ra'oi and ma'oi more thinly. The standard grammar rejects all of them. None is official.

section.title: Repairs and terminators: lo'ai, sa'ai, le'ai and others
section.para: The following experimental cmavo are discussed in this section:

cmavo-entry.description: close everything back to the main bridi

section.para: error correctionexperimental quote set lo'aisa'aile'aiThe erasure words of standard Lojban (see ) can only erase the most recent words. But in live conversation, people often want to reach back and repair something that they said a sentence ago. The error-correction quotes lo'ai, sa'ai, and le'ai do that, and the community count of 2015 placed them among its half-dozen most frequent experimental words, beside the quotation words of . The set works like a search-and-replace: lo'ai quotes the wrong text, sa'ai quotes its replacement, and le'ai closes the correction:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi klama lo zarci .i lo'ai zarci sa'ai zdani le'ai
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I go-to a market. - [wrong:] market [replace:] house [end]
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I went to the market – I mean, the house.

section.para: The two quoted parts may come in either order, and either may be left out when context supplies it. A bare le'ai on its own simply admits that a mistake was made somewhere, and leaves the listener to find it.

iaui'auA different kind of repair is wanted when a sentence has wandered deep into subordinate clauses and the speaker wants to add something to the main bridi. In standard Lojban that takes a string of terminators, each matched to a construct that is still open, and in speech the count is easy to lose. The word iau (also spelled i'au, the form from which the shorter one was derived) closes every open construct at once and returns to the top level of the sentence, as .i would, without starting a new sentence:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi djica lo nu do klama lo zarci iau ca lo cabdei
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I want the event-of your going-to the market [back-to-top] at the today.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I want you to go to the market; today, I mean.

section.para: Without the iau, the time tag would fall inside the nu clause and say when the going happens, not when the wanting does. An attitudinal placed right after iau is understood to apply to the whole sentence, which gives afterthought attitudinals a home.

cu'auThe word cu'au goes one step further and makes the terminators interchangeable. It looks back for the most recently opened construct that is still open and acts as whatever terminator would close it; its dictionary entry illustrates this with lo broda cu'au cu'au for lo broda ku vau. Its proponents subscript it to close several constructs at once. It has had a modest following since 2014, and no parser we tried accepts it, so this book records it by description only.

ze'eiThe last word in this section belongs here only loosely, since it makes other words rather than repairing them. ze'ei binds two arbitrary words into one nonce word: the word on its left supplies the meaning, and the word on its right supplies the grammar. A speaker who wants a new abstractor, say, can glue a gismu to nu with ze'ei and use the result wherever nu would go, without first finding a free experimental cmavo shape. Its dictionary entry puts it in selma'o SI, beside the erasure word, though it erases nothing.
The correction set is among the most common experimental constructions in genuine text. iau, cu'au and ze'ei each have real but much thinner use. None is official.

section.title: New attitudinals and indicators
section.para: The following experimental cmavo are discussed in this section:

cmavo-entry.description: contour: stronger over time; nai: weaker over time
previous word is a nonce creation
simply, merely; nai: there is more to it
imagining, roleplaying; nai: in real life
previous lujvo is regular in meaning

section.para: attitudinalsexperimentalThe indicators of form a closed system, and that chapter itself describes the system as tentative. The community has treated the invitation seriously: of all the parts of the language, the indicators have attracted the most experimental cmavo, and chat text in particular is full of them. This section gives the ones that this edition's editors met most often, by the kind of indicator that each one is.

xo'o warns that attitudinals are meant sincerely, never ironically, and xo'o fills exactly that gap. It is an attitudinal modifier, like dai or pei, and it marks the preceding attitudinal (or the whole utterance, when it stands alone) as sarcastic. Its negative form xo'o nai insists on sincerity. The word was chosen for its resemblance to zo'o:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: .ui xo'o lo carvi cu di'a cfari
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Oh, joy. The rain is starting again.

section.para: au'uuu'ixu'oTwo new pure emotions have a following: au'u, the feeling that something is cute, with au'u nai for the repulsively uncute; and uu'i, which fuses .uu and .u'i into schadenfreude, pleasure at someone else's misfortune. The word xu'o is a contour rather than an emotion: placed after an attitudinal, it says that the feeling is growing stronger, and xu'o nai says that it is fading. Standard Lojban can say how strong a feeling is () but not which way it is heading.

da'oida'eiThe modifier dai of says that an attitude belongs to someone other than the speaker, without saying whom. The word da'oi, defined in selma'o DOI, takes a sumti and says whose attitude it is:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: .ui da'oi la .alis. lo xirma cu bajra
interlinear-gloss.natlang: The horse is running, to Alice's delight.

section.para: Its companion da'ei attributes the cause of a feeling rather than its owner: .iu followed by da'ei do is love that you cause, which is to say I love you. It has fewer users than da'oi, and no parser we tried accepts it.

ja'aitoi'eTwo small words act on indicators and on other cmavo. ja'ai is the affirmative counterpart of nai: attached to a cmavo, it affirms it, by the same analogy that gives ja'a to na and je'a to na'e (see ). It is useful in answers, where .e ja'ai affirms a connective that the question had offered as .e nai; it was first suggested in 1999 and has been in the dictionary since 2005. toi'e opens a parenthesis of indicators that apply to the indicator just before it, instead of to the surrounding text, so that one can be amused at one's own anger rather than at the world. Standard Lojban has no way to point one indicator at another.
si'auAmong the evidentials of , the community has found one gap in particular: there is no plain it seems that. si'au supplies it, and it is one of the most frequent experimental words in chat:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: It seems the weather is going to change.

section.para: zi'axe'oxa'ixu'ava'oiThe new discursives are a mixed bag. zi'a, placed after a word, flags it as a nonce creation that may not be standard; it does the job of za'e from , but as an indicator that follows its word rather than a marker that precedes it, and coiners use it often. xe'o means simply or merely, with the sense that there is nothing more to the matter, and xe'o nai warns that there is more to it; its author contrasts it with po'o, which restricts, and sa'u, which only simplifies. xa'i marks an utterance as imagined or role-played, the equivalent of the asterisked actions of online chat, and xa'i nai steps back out of character. xu'a marks that the speaker is arguing a point, with xu'a nai for conceding one. va'oi asserts that the lujvo just before it has the regular meaning that its parts predict (a jvajvo in community jargon), and va'oi nai warns that it does not.

ko'oiko'oi is the imperative or hortative discursive. Standard Lojban commands only through ko, which can command nobody but the listener. With ko'oi any bridi becomes a command or a wish that it be true, so that ko itself can be analyzed as do plus ko'oi, and mi'o klama ko'oi is let's go. It is broader than any single member of the .e'o family (), which is both its virtue and its vagueness.

All these words appear in genuine text, xo'o, si'au, zi'a, da'oi and ja'ai often, the others more thinly. No parser we tried accepts da'ei, toi'e, xu'o, zi'a, xe'o, xa'i or xu'a in a sentence, so they appear here by description only. None is official.

section.title: New vocatives and interjection makers
section.para: The following experimental cmavo are discussed in this section:

cmavo-entry.description: nonce interjection from the next word
greeting or parting, as context decides

section.para: vocativesexperimentalki'aiThe vocatives of selma'o COI () are the closest thing standard Lojban has to interjections, and the community has stretched them in two directions. The first is a small family of converters, which turn an ordinary word into an interjection on the spot. ki'ai, from krixa, is the general one: it takes a following selbri, cmevla or zoi quotation and makes a nonce exclamation of it. A speaker who feels wonder can therefore shout it without waiting for an attitudinal to be assigned:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Wow! You won.

section.para: sa'eici'oiIts two narrower siblings take a cmevla or a zoi quotation. sa'ei makes it an onomatopoeia, a sound effect in the manner of comic books; ci'oi makes it a psychomime, a word that imitates a state of mind or a manner rather than a sound, a category that Japanese has in abundance and English barely has at all. Since the converted word is a name, it carries the dots of a cmevla:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Bam! The box fell.

section.para: di'aiThe second direction adds vocatives with new meanings. di'ai expresses a wish for the good of the person addressed; di'ai nai is a curse. It says in one word what standard Lojban must build from .a'o and a bridi:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Good luck to you!

section.para: o'aia'oico'oiThree more greetings circulate, and the first two are playful coinages on English words, of the kind the community calls a u'ivla. o'ai is a slightly surprised greeting; a'oi is a slightly piratical one, from ahoy; and co'oi combines coi with co'o into a greeting-or-parting that context resolves, for the passing hi that is also a bye. All three are common in chat, where greetings are frequent and brevity is prized.

xu'edialoguespeaker tags inThe word xu'e solves a problem of written dialogue. Lojban has no quotation marks to switch speakers, and sei ko'a cusku is long. xu'e followed by a sumti tags the sentence as that person's words, so that a dialogue can run xu'e la .alis., then Alice's sentence, then xu'e la .bob., and so on. It comes from the Loglan word hue with the same job. No parser we tried accepts it, so no example sentence appears here.
Genuine text attests all eight, ki'ai, sa'ei, di'ai, o'ai, a'oi and co'oi often, ci'oi and xu'e less so. None is official.

section.title: New pro-sumti, articles and conversions
section.para: The following experimental cmavo are discussed in this section:

cmavo-entry.description: they: the last two or more sumti together
we: the speaker and at least one other
repeat the last bridi containing the quoted word
third place to first, others unchanged
selbri from a tag (inverse of fi'o)

section.para: xaimi'aixa'uThe pro-sumti of leave a few gaps that speakers kept tripping over. ri repeats one sumti; there is no short way to repeat two of them together, which is what English they does after Alice saw Bob. The word xai does exactly that: it refers back to two or more preceding sumti, taken together.

interlinear-gloss.jbo: la .alis. pu viska la .bob. .i xai ca tavla
interlinear-gloss.gloss: That-named Alice [past] sees that-named Bob. - They [present] talk.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Alice saw Bob. Now they are talking.

section.para: In the same spirit, mi'ai is a general we: the speaker and at least one other person, without the commitment to including or excluding the listener that mi'o, mi'a and ma'a each carry. Its author treats those three as special cases of it. xa'u, a recent coinage after a Loglan word, refers to the situation that is about to follow, as in watch this; its use is not yet established.

go'oiThe pro-bridi go'oi repeats a bridi by content rather than by position. It quotes the next word, as zo would, and stands for the most recent bridi that contained that word. Where go'i can only reach the previous sentence, go'oi can reach back several, as long as the speaker remembers a word from the one wanted.

zo'ei The word zo'ei (with a grammar like LAhE) means something associated with ..., roughly zo'e pe. It often takes the place of a tu'a that a lazy speaker stretches beyond its abstraction sense. For example, mi viska zo'ei la .paris. means I see something related to Paris: a photograph, perhaps, or the skyline.

A caveat about the shape of the word. In standard Lojban, zo quotes whatever single word follows it, and a parser that does not know zo'ei as a word has every right to read it as zo followed by the quoted word 'ei. The danger is silent. The sentence above still parses that way, with an entirely different structure, so make sure that your tool knows the word before you trust its reading.
mo'oiri'oiTwo experimental articles join the descriptors of . mo'oi is the interrogative article which, roughly ma noi but without starting a new bridi:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Which book do you like?

section.para: ri'oi is an anaphoric article: ri'oi cukta is the most recently mentioned thing that is a book, the job that English gives to the after a first mention (compare bi'unai in , and see for the argument around it):

interlinear-gloss.natlang: The book I mentioned is good.

section.para: to'aija'eixo'ibei'eThe remaining words rearrange places. to'ai is a conversion in the manner of , but it moves the third place to the front and leaves the others in their order, which te does not do: to'ai dunda has the recipient first, then the giver, then the gift, the same effect as te se dunda. ja'ei is to la'e what jai is to tu'a: it converts a selbri so that its first place takes the referent of what the sumti refers to. xo'i undoes fi'o, extracting the selbri from a tag, so that xo'i applied to bau gives bangu. And bei'e opens a run of linked sumti that fill the places of the preceding selbri in order, until be'o, which saves the repeated bei of . Of these four, to'ai and xo'i have had the most use, and no parser we tried accepts xo'i or bei'e.

Genuine text attests xai, mi'ai, zo'ei, mo'oi, ri'oi and go'oi with some regularity, the others thinly. The top definitions of xa'u and ja'ei are recent, and most of the recorded uses of those spellings predate them. None is official.

section.title: Abstraction and predicates
section.para: The following experimental cmavo are discussed in this section:

cmavo-entry.description: x1 is such that [bridi], binding ke'a
x1, x2, ... satisfy [bridi], binding the ce'u slots
abstract predicate from a selbri (all places ce'u)
predicate from an abstract predicate sumti
lambda prenex: end of bound-variable list
description from a whole bridi, with ke'a
sumti referring to a whole bridi

section.para: abstractionexperimental abstractorspoi'iThe abstractors of turn a bridi into an event, a property or a proposition. A family of experimental words turns a bridi into other things. The oldest is poi'i, proposed around 2001: poi'i ke'a broda is the thing that is such that the bridi is true of it, with ke'a marking the place, exactly as in a relative clause. It makes a selbri out of any bridi, so that a description need not be rebuilt around the right gismu:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi nelci lo poi'i ke'a dunda lo cukta mi
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I like the one-such-that IT gives the book to-me.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I like whoever gave me the book.

section.para: kai'uThe abstractor kai'u does the same with several places at once: its x1, x2 and so on are bound to the ce'u slots of its bridi, in order, so that mi do kai'u ce'u ce'u prami is a roundabout mi prami do. Its purpose is to let a sentence state a relation as a relation.

me'eime'auThe pair me'ei and me'au go back and forth between a selbri and the abstract predicate it expresses. me'ei is an article: me'ei prami is the relation of loving, with every place left open, which is to say lo ka ce'u ce'u prami. me'au is its inverse and belongs with me (): it takes a sumti that refers to an abstract predicate and uses it as a selbri again, so that mi me'au lo ka ce'u klama lo zarci is just mi klama lo zarci. Put together, the two let a conversation talk about a predicate and then apply it:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: me'ei prami cu vajni .i mi me'au ri do
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Loving matters. I do it to you.

section.para: The dictionary's own gloss of me'au calls it essentially ckaji with any number of places, which is the clearest short description. me'au is among the most frequent experimental words in the archived chat logs.

ce'aiThe word ce'ai is a prenex marker, like zo'u (), for use inside a ka abstraction. The variables listed before it are the bound places of the property, in order, and the bridi after it may use them by name. It replaces repeated ce'u goi ko'a assignments and keeps nested properties apart:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi'o simxu lo ka ko'a ko'e ce'ai ko'a prami ko'e
interlinear-gloss.gloss: We-two mutual-in the property it-1 it-2 [where:] it-1 loves it-2.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: You and I love each other.

section.para: lo'oixu'uku'auFinally, a small selma'o of its own, LOhOI*, makes sumti directly out of bridi. lo'oi is the full-bridi equivalent of lo: lo'oi ke'a bevri lo pipno ku'au describes whatever carries the piano, with ke'a marking the described place and ku'au as the elidable terminator. Its sibling xu'u makes a sumti that refers to the bridi itself, without picking out a place, which is what lo su'u does in standard Lojban at the cost of two words. Both have had modest but steady use, and xu'u reappears in , where one dialect gives it a shorter spelling.
Genuine text attests all of these, me'au, me'ei and ce'ai most often. None is official.

section.title: Connectives, adverbials and negation
section.para: The following experimental cmavo are discussed in this section:

adverbialsexperimentalxoiLojban has no adverbs. An English slowly becomes a tanru, a tense, or a whole clause ( and ), and all three change the shape of the sentence. Several experimental words try to add an adverbial that can be dropped into a sentence as freely as an indicator. The most used is xoi, which takes a following selbri (and any terms before it) and makes a free phrase of it that modifies the main predicate:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: I walk slowly.

section.para: The word has had a long and crowded life: the dictionary has carried definitions of it in four different selma'o, and the one with the most votes, from 2025, revised an older adverbial clause sense after that sense was declared obsolete. Text from before then uses xoi to enclose a whole bridi, so the reader of older material should expect either.

poi'anoi'aThe pair poi'a and noi'a, from 2016, is more precise about what it claims. Each converts a selbri into an adverbial term whose first place is the event of the outer bridi, and each has the elidable terminator fe'u. poi'a is restrictive, like poi: broda poi'a brode claims that the event of broda happens and is a brode. noi'a is incidental, like noi: it claims broda, and remarks separately that the event is a brode:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi klama lo zarci poi'a sutra
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I go to the market quickly.

section.para: ji'oice'oijo'oiThree words extend the connectives of . ji'oi takes a predicate of at least two places and turns it into a connective with the grammar of JA, the predicate stating the relation between the two connected propositions; its terminator is te'u. So mi ji'oi balvi do snada says that my succeeding comes after your succeeding. Its author notes that it has no forethought or sumti-connective form, so its users generally pair it with the connective reforms described on the community wiki. ce'oi is a non-logical connective that separates the arguments of a function, where ce'o would wrongly suggest a sequence. jo'oi connects two sentences as the more ..., the more ...; its definition is very recent and its use so far is slight.

na'eina'ei is a scalar-negation word with the force of contradictory negation: mi na'ei klama denies that I go, as mi na klama does, but as a modifier of the selbri rather than of the bridi, where na'e () would only say that I do something other than go. Its author states the quantifier laws of with it: not all of them go is some of them na'ei go.
Genuine text attests xoi very often, in several of its senses, and the rest in smaller numbers. None is official.

section.title: Plural quantifiers: su'oi and ro'oi
section.para: The following experimental cmavo are discussed in this section:

plural quantificationsu'oiro'oiThe official quantifiers su'o and ro are singular. A variable that they bind stands for one individual at a time (see ). That leaves a genuine gap, since some predicates are true of several things taken together but of no one of them alone. Gather, surround, and be a twosome are examples. A claim like some people are gathering cannot be built from a singular quantifier at all, because no single person gathers.
Standard Lojban fills the gap with constants. An unquantified lo prenu can refer to people jointly, and loi forms groups. But standard Lojban has no way to quantify plurally.
The experimental pair su'oi and ro'oi supplies exactly that. A variable bound by them can stand for one or more things at once. With them, you can say:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: su'oi da poi prenu cu jmaji
interlinear-gloss.natlang: Some people are gathering.

section.para: Here the da stands for the gatherers jointly. Each member of the pair can be defined from the other by the usual duality: su'oi da is na ku ro'oi da na ku. This parallels the singular rules of exactly. The logic chapters of this book use only the official singular quantifiers.

section.title: Tags, tenses and numbers
section.para: The following experimental cmavo are discussed in this section:

cmavo-entry.description: at the same online place as
the n-th date or time unit from a reference point

section.para: xauka'aiThe modal tags of are built from gismu, and two further ones are common enough to mention. xau marks the beneficiary of the bridi, for the benefit of; standard Lojban says the same with se va'u, and its author gives that as the nearest equivalent. ka'ai, from kansa, tags a companion: mi klama ka'ai do is I go with you. No parser we tried accepts xau in a sentence.

xa'oThe event contours of have a small asymmetry. za'o covers the stretch of an event that drags on past its natural end; its mirror image, an event already under way before its natural beginning, has no standard contour. The word xa'o, in the dictionary since 2003 and among the most highly voted of all experimental cmavo, fills that slot:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: The child is awake ahead of time.

section.para: xei'eThe newest tense in this chapter is a child of the internet. xei'e is a spatial tense, like bu'u, that locates an event at the same online place as its sumti: the same chat channel, forum or site. It appeared in 2020 and its use is confined, naturally, to online conversation.

xo'e Among numbers, the word xo'e is the elliptical digit, and it has more votes in the dictionary than any other experimental cmavo. It is to numbers what zo'e is to sumti: an unspecified quantity that the speaker chooses not to give:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: Some number of people are coming.

section.para: xeitau'upi'aimoi'oThe rest of the mathematical words are for specialists. xei is a second spelling of the hexadecimal digit E, which gives as rei; its users find rei too easy to mishear as re. tau'u is the constant tau, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its radius, which is twice pi. pi'ai multiplies unit selbri in forethought: placed before xampo and snidu, it names the ampere-second, or coulomb. And moi'o is a MOI word for dates: no moi'o of a day is today, and pa moi'o of a month is next month, counted from a reference point that defaults to now. No parser we tried accepts xei, tau'u or pi'ai.
Genuine text attests xo'e and xa'o regularly and the others in small numbers; pi'ai's use is concentrated in 2012–2015. None is official.

section.title: Announcing a dialect: jo'au
section.para: The following experimental cmavo is discussed in this section:

cmavo-entry.description: the following text is in dialect ...

section.para: dialectsannouncing with jo'aujo'auThe words so far in this chapter add to standard Lojban without changing it: a text that uses them is still standard text with some extra words in it. The rest of this chapter describes variants that reinterpret standard forms, and a reader who meets such a text without warning will misread it in silence. The community's answer is a header. The vocative jo'au, defined in 2015 as change version/dialect, is followed by a name for the dialect and, if needed, by the elidable terminator do'u; its dictionary entry asks for it at the very start of a text, and says that it applies until the next jo'au:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: What follows is in the tcekitaujau dialect.

section.para: This book treats jo'au as a convention between writers and readers, and nothing more. Its definition speaks of changing the dialect of a parser, and lists parsers by name as possible arguments, but this book does not rely on any tool to act on the header, and does not know of one that does anything useful with it. What the header does reliably is tell a human reader that the usual meanings are suspended, which is exactly what the dialects below need.
The header is the convention that the authors of the dialects below asked their readers to use, and a modest number of texts and chat lines carry it. It is not official.

section.title: Other takes on the articles
section.para: articlesalternative accounts ofgadrialternative accounts ofThe articles of are the one part of the language that an LLG vote has changed since the first edition, and teaches the ratified account. This section describes two other ways of using the same words that a reader will meet in practice. Neither is official, and neither changes what this book teaches; they are here because a reader of real text must be able to recognize them. The first is a written proposal with a name; the second is a habit with no author at all.

gadganzuThe proposal is called gadganzu, from gadri and ganzu, organize. It was written on the community wiki in June and July 2015 by two people known by their Lojban names, la zipcpi and la cadgu'a, and its idea is to give the rarer articles sharp and distinct jobs while leaving the ratified lo and la alone. Its authors described the result as a spectrum from the most definite to the least, and the table gives it in that order, with the new mass forms beside the individual ones:

cmavo-entry.description: demonstrative: this or that ... (reassigned; lei'i new)
deictic: the ... that are identifiable or knowable (tightened)
essentialist: the ideal model of ... (reassigned; loi'i new)

section.para: What gadganzu keeps from the ratified account is its core: lo, loi, la and lai are untouched, and one of its authors said in chat that its foundation was the ratified system. What it reassigns are the three set articles and the stereotype article: le'i becomes a demonstrative, roughly ti noi or ta noi without the distance and without a new clause; le'e becomes an anaphoric article that its authors call essentially identical to lo bi'unai broda; and lo'i becomes the essentialist article, the Platonic model of a thing. Sets, the authors say, are hardly ever needed in conversation, and for those who need them there is lu'i. What it adds are the five mass forms in the table, the interrogative pair, and a titular relative clause voi'i, for Alexander the Great, that lives beside voi. The proposal also claims to leave le alone apart from a tightened definition. That claim deserves a second look: the ratified text says that le describes what the speaker has in mind, while gadganzu's le is what is identifiable or knowable, which leans toward the listener instead. The two readings agree in most sentences and part company in exactly the cases discussed below.

Because gadganzu gives standard words new meanings, a sentence in it means something else to a standard reader. The authors therefore asked their readers to mark such text with the header jo'au gadganzu of . Under that header, the following says that this book is beautiful; without it, under the ratified rules, it says that a set of books is:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: This book is beautiful.

section.para: A handful of speakers used gadganzu, mainly in chat in 2015 and again in 2019–2021, and one wiki translation carries its header. It was never brought before the BPFK. Its critics objected on different grounds: that the four meanings of lo which motivated it can be told apart with the standard devices of scope, variables and attitudinals; that reassigning any current article is too high a price; and that the system is too complex to learn. A participant in its design added that it sharpens a few central articles without extending the same principles to all of them.

leas English "the"theand leThe second take needs no table. Many learners, and some teaching texts, simply use lo for English a and le for English the: introduce a thing with lo, and refer back to it with le. This book's own chapter on sumti says that le is quite close in meaning to English the, so the habit has an honest pedigree, and in a great many sentences it does no harm at all:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi viska lo mlatu .i le mlatu cu cmalu
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I see a cat. - The cat - is-small.
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I see a cat. The cat is small.

section.para: The sentence is good standard Lojban under the ratified rules too, because the speaker does have a specific cat in mind by the second sentence. The argument against the habit is about what the two words track. English the tracks the listener: it says that the listener can already identify the thing, usually because it was mentioned before. Lojban le tracks the speaker: it says that the speaker has particular things in mind, whether or not the listener knows which ( says this in as many words). So le can introduce something brand new, which the cannot, and the aforementioned has its own marker in Lojban, the discursive bi'unai, with bi'u for the new (). The generic the of the wolf is endangered is lo, and a repeated lo may refer to the same thing as the first one. Whether a repeat mention is better served by le or by lo is a point on which fluent speakers have disagreed in public, and nothing official settles it.

It is an observation of this edition's editors, from reading present-day text and attributing nothing to a survey, that most of the le one meets today follows one of the two takes in this section: either the gadganzu reading or the plain definite article. The ratified account of remains what this book teaches, and a reader who follows it will be understood by users of both.

Gadganzu is a written proposal from 2015 that no official body considered; a small number of identifiable speakers used it. The reading of le as a plain definite article is a learner's habit and a teaching shortcut, attested in first-person statements on the mailing lists and in chat, and it was never proposed as a rule.

The meanings of lo and le themselves are ratified, and this section does not change them. Which article best serves a repeat mention is an open question among speakers, and this edition's choice to teach the ratified account does not settle it for the language.

section.title: The cmevla-brivla merger
section.para: cmevla-brivla mergerThe dialects discussed so far add words or reinterpret meanings. The remaining two change the grammar. The cmevla-brivla merger (CBM) removes the grammatical wall between name words and predicate words. Under it, a cmevla like .djan. can serve as a selbri or as a tanru unit. It then predicates of its subject, and the users of the dialect decide its precise place structure. In addition, the article la becomes an ordinary descriptor, which takes whatever selbri follows it.

The motivating complaint is a pedagogical one. In standard Lojban, la behaves one way before a cmevla and another way before a brivla. Learners who discover that predicates can name things are tempted to write what the standard grammar forbids. The standard grammar rejects the following sentence, but under CBM it is fine:

interlinear-gloss.natlang: This John-s, so to speak. (CBM dialect only)

section.para: The merger reinterprets existing forms; it does not merely add new ones. It is therefore not backward-compatible: the same string of standard Lojban can parse differently under CBM. More than one parser implements the dialect, under an explicit switch or as a separate grammar, and the implementations differ in some corners in how aggressively they reinterpret la phrases. They agree on the new permission itself: a cmevla can predicate.
CBM is a real dialect, parsers implement it, and it has an established design literature. In the tools that implement it, it requires an explicit dialect grammar or switch.

section.title: Short words for common meanings: tcekitau and jboponei
section.para: tcekitauce-ki-tau-jaucmavo swapsThe last family of dialects consists of cmavo swaps, and it starts from a complaint about the allocation of short words. The cmavo of one syllable are the most precious real estate in the language, and some of them do very little. The letteral shifts of and some of the more exotic mathematical cmavo of see little or no use in ordinary text, yet each holds a form of the shape CV or CVV. Meanwhile some of the busiest cmavo in the language have two syllables: ce'u, ke'a, tu'a, jo'u and du'u. The swap proposals try to reclaim the idle short forms for more productive meanings, and since they take existing words away from their official senses, they are dialects in the full sense: text in them means something else to a standard reader.

The main example, and the most popular, is the family that the dictionary calls tcekitau, after the first three swapped words ce, ki and tau; the wiki page that proposed it in 2014 calls the full version tcekitaujau, or ce-ki-tau-jau in English. Its primary proposal swaps five pairs. In tcekitau text, ce means what ce'u means in this book, ki means ke'a, tau means tu'a, jau means jo'u, and du means du'u; and in each case the reverse, so that the long forms take over the old meanings of the short ones. In principle each swap works in both directions, and speakers can adopt each one separately. The wiki page lists a long second tier of further possible swaps, from su'o to su to the connective reforms, and the dictionary word tcekitau names the whole class rather than any one selection. The page itself records the main criticism: the proposal breaks compatibility with every existing text in exchange for shorter spellings, and fixes nothing that was broken.

Here is the trap. Most of the short forms also have meanings in standard Lojban, so a swapped sentence often parses in both grammars, with different meanings. Take lo broda poi ki broda. To a standard parser it is a sticky-tense construction; to a tcekitau parser it is a relative clause with ke'a. Text in this dialect is therefore unintelligible to a standard reader in a peculiarly silent way: nothing fails, but the text means something else. A writer avoids the trap by announcing the dialect first, with the header jo'au tcekitaujau of .

A later summary on the community wiki, from 2021, makes an observation worth passing on: in practice the swaps mostly went one way. Speakers who adopted ce for ce'u went on using ce'u too, and almost nobody used the long forms in their new, swapped meanings, so the effect was to make synonyms rather than to exchange them. That is one observer's report, with no count behind it.

jboponeipoin jboponeineiin jboponeiA second, smaller swap dialect is jboponei, named from lojbo and the two words it reassigns. Its author introduced it in chat in 2018 with a complaint of his own: a learner must choose among nu, ka and du'u at every abstraction, while su'u, the general abstractor, would cover them all but is longer to write and to say. In jboponei the possessive po of is reassigned to mean lo su'u, the general abstraction taken as a sumti (or xu'u of , which means the same), and the pro-bridi nei of becomes its terminator. The old sense of po is said with a relative clause instead, and the old sense of nei is given to zi'e, which the connective reforms that this dialect's users also follow had made redundant:

interlinear-gloss.jbo: mi djica po do klama nei
interlinear-gloss.gloss: I want [abstraction:] you go [end]. (jboponei dialect only)
interlinear-gloss.natlang: I want you to go.

section.para: To a standard parser the sentence is simply ungrammatical, which is at least safer than the silent misreading of tcekitau. The dialect had one committed user and a few occasional ones in chat from 2018 on, and other speakers' verdicts there ran from amusement to the flat judgment that it is strange. It is in this book as the smallest complete example of what a swap dialect does: it takes one common two-word phrase and gives it a one-syllable spelling that already belonged to something else.

This book includes the swap dialects as the clearest worked examples of what a dialect is. Both are written proposals that no official body considered, with a handful of users each. The text of this book uses none of the swaps.
